correctness.rationale: Exact eventual periodicity gives an annihilator E^N(E^L-1), and the second-order recurrence gives a common rational annihilator of degree <=2. Cyclotomic factor degrees leave precisely the six recurrence shapes. [2,1] and [4,2] enforce a|b and, in period 3/6, b|a; the nonzero condition removes one sign each. Remaining periodic cases are explicitly strong-GCD, transient cases divisor-chains; the cited binomid-pyramid sufficiency theorems then establish every-level integrality. Divisibility conversely yields a|b and b|f4. Sharpness witnesses are explicit, and the finite checker passed 984 parameter cases plus accepted-family samples.

originality.rationale: The 2023 motivating article states the unrestricted recurrence binomid-versus-divisible question and supplies only the strong-GCD/divisor-chain sufficient directions; the 1985 paper classifies strong divisibility, without showing the two small binomid integrality tests imply divisibility. The new assertion is a sharp finite recognition theorem for all exactly eventually periodic second-order recurrences, including the weakly but not strongly divisible transient cases. This is not a restatement of the pre-existing strong-divisibility families. No equivalent claim appeared in targeted research-record or publication searches.

value.rationale: Shapiro (2023) explicitly asks whether second-order binomid sequences must be divisible. The theorem resolves a natural complete dynamical subclass, all exactly eventually periodic solutions including transient cases, through only two finite integrality checks; moreover it gives a sharp row-four recognition cutoff and upgrades first-level integrality to the entire binomid pyramid. It is not merely a new example, parameter renaming, or a table recomputation: the statement is an equivalence for an infinite, structurally defined class and separates its finite test from prior stronger premises.
